standard.title: Global Influences on Post-War Australia
standard.description: causes and effects of the significant events and developments of the major global influences on Australia in the post-Second World War period
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the causes and effects of major global events in earlier periods, including WWI and the Great Depression, and their impact on Australia.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse the causes and effects of major global influences on Australia in the post-WWII period, including the Cold War, the long economic boom, cultural change, and the environmental movement.

nodes.label: The Cold War and Australia
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how the fear of communism and the emergence of the Cold War impacted on Australian society, particularly in relation to political debates, immigration and popular culture.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how the Cold War affected at least two aspects of Australian society — political, immigration, or cultural.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how the fear of communism and the Cold War impacted Australia: political debates including the Communist Party Dissolution Bill, the Petrov Affair, and the DLP split; immigration screening and the exclusion of perceived communist sympathisers; aspects of popular culture including music, film, and sport as sites of ideological competition; explain how Cold War anxiety shaped both government policy and everyday Australian attitudes.
wider: Investigate the Petrov Affair (1954) in depth — examining what happened, how it was used politically by the Menzies government, and what it reveals about the relationship between genuine security concerns and political exploitation of Cold War fear

Examine how Cold War propaganda shaped Australian popular culture in the 1950s — analysing films, public information campaigns, and media coverage to understand how ideological messages were embedded in everyday cultural life
nodes.hinge_reason: The Cold War context established here underpins K17's analysis of Vietnam's impact on Australia and K18's examination of how Australians questioned traditional values in the 1960s–70s. Students who do not understand the Cold War framework cannot make sense of why Vietnam became so politically divisive.

response_modes.reason: Cold War anxiety operated across multiple domains simultaneously — political, cultural, social. Structure the analysis so students can see how a single ideological context (fear of communism) produced effects across seemingly unrelated areas of Australian life.

success_criteria: Explain how the Cold War affected Australian political debates, identifying at least one specific event or controversy
Describe how Cold War anxiety influenced Australian immigration policy
Explain how the Cold War was reflected in aspects of Australian popular culture

nodes.label: The long boom and cultural change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the long economic boom under Menzies and analyse how post-war prosperity produced cultural change, including the development of youth culture in the 1960s.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the main features of the long boom and explain how post-war prosperity contributed to the development of youth culture.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the 'long boom' under Menzies — the expansion of primary industry exports (wool, iron ore), the growth of protected manufacturing (steel, textiles, electrical goods, automobiles), the promotion of home ownership; analyse the post-WWII baby boom and its cultural consequences including the development of youth culture in the 1960s; investigate American and British cultural influences — television for the Melbourne Olympics (1956), Bill Haley's Australian tour (1957), the Mersey sound and The Beatles' tour (1964); examine competing perspectives on rock 'n' roll, film and television across age, gender, and values — conservatism vs rebellion, challenge to established ideas and national identity.
wider: Examine the development of television in Australia from 1956 as a case study in how a new medium transformed both cultural consumption and political communication, comparing its early years with its later role in the Vietnam War coverage and the 1967 Referendum

Compare conservative and progressive perspectives on rock 'n' roll culture in the late 1950s and 1960s, examining what the cultural conflict reveals about the generational tensions that would become politically significant in the late 1960s

response_modes.reason: The long boom and cultural change are most meaningfully taught in combination — prosperity created the conditions for youth culture and consumerism, which in turn created the generational tensions that explain the political upheavals of the late 1960s and 1970s addressed in K18.

success_criteria: Describe the main features of the long economic boom under Menzies
Explain how post-war prosperity contributed to the development of youth culture in the 1960s
Describe the American and British cultural influences on Australia in the 1950s–60s and explain competing responses to those influences

nodes.label: The environmental movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the causes and conditions that led to the environmental movement in Australia and globally, and explain its effects on changing public opinion.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two causes of the environmental movement and describe at least one effect on public opinion or policy.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the causes and conditions that led to the environmental movement: rapid population increase, urbanisation, increases in industrial pollution and waste, and species extinction; explain the effects on changing public opinion about protecting the environment; connect to K14's examination of how environmental perspectives shifted from fringe concern to mainstream agenda.
wider: Examine the causes and conditions specifically through Australian environmental campaigns (e.g. the Franklin Dam campaign, the Great Barrier Reef protection movement), analysing how local campaigns connected to global environmental awareness

Investigate how the environmental movement intersected with First Nations land rights campaigns in Australia, examining cases where environmental protection and Indigenous land claims reinforced each other

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the global influences of the Cold War and cultural change with the environmental movement — connecting three post-war global developments that each reshaped Australian society. It also connects forward to K17's treatment of international environmental treaties.

success_criteria: Identify at least two causes of the environmental movement
Explain how the environmental movement changed public opinion about at least one specific issue
Connect the emergence of the environmental movement to broader post-war developments examined in this standard
